to become; whom Apollonius, as is likely, also follows. But Thales (cf. 11 A 12 Diels-Kranz) posited water as the principle of all things, taking it from the poet who says (H 99): 'but may you all become water and earth.' And Zeno (fg 104 Arn.) says that the chaos in Hesiod (Theog. 116 sq.) is water, from the settling of which mud comes to be, and when this solidifies the earth is made firm; and third, Eros came to be according to Hesiod (ib. 120), in order to represent fire; for love is a rather fiery passion. Anaxagoras (cf. 59 A 72 Diels-Kranz) says that the sun is a red-hot mass, from which all things come to be. Therefore Euripides (Or. 983), who was his pupil, says that the sun is a golden clod. And the same Anaxagoras (59 A 77 Diels-Kranz) declares that the moon is a broad land, from which the Nemean lion is thought to have fallen.

501. Mountains: Duris (76 fg 87 J.) says that the stones brought down by the Giants, those that fell into the sea became islands, and those that fell on the land became mountains.
509. Dictaean: Cretan, where Zeus was reared, as Callimachus (Hymn. I 4 sqq.) also relates.

513-15a. But they unceasingly: instead of 'unceasingly' and 'insatiably.' The sense: when the song ceased, still unsatisfied with it, they had stretched their heads forward with ears pricked up and were keeping quiet in stillness; such was the pleasure that held them.
b. Such for them: such pleasure did he impose on those listening to him. L
516-18a. Nor even after mixing: the phrase must be read thus: 'then not even after mixing nor after a time,' meaning 'immediately and after a little while.'
